description: This cluster provides a comprehensive overview of the wide range of operational risk types encountered in the maritime sector and the diverse approaches used to assess and manage them. The studies address physical risks such as operational delays, port congestion, equipment failures, cargo loss and environmental events, as well as information-based and structural risks arising from communication gaps, information deficiencies and digitalization-related uncertainties. The analyses rely on expert judgment, statistical data and various analytical techniques, reflecting an effort to develop a holistic understanding of risk management in maritime operations. The methodological approaches in this cluster are highly diverse. Fan et al. (2024) analyze the impact of naval escorts on piracy risk in East Africa using Tree Augmented Naive Bayesian Networks (TAN). Fu et al. (2023) propose a resilience-oriented, four-stage functional framework for risk management in Arctic ice-covered waters. Kayisoglu et al. (2022) investigate the cybersecurity of the Electronic Chart Display and Information System (ECDIS) by defining navigator responsibilities and estimating human error probabilities using the Success Likelihood Index Method (SLIM) based Human Reliability Analysis (HRA). Liu et al. (2024a) introduce an enhanced Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA) supported by expert belief networks, showing improved handling of uncertainty. Mohsendokht et al. (2024) develop a data-driven Bayesian Network (BN) model to identify critical factors in terrorist attack scenarios and support maritime security decision-making. Nezamian and Kartsounis (2019) propose a risk-based asset management framework for maintaining the structural integrity of port infrastructures, integrating digital data collection tools to optimize maintenance. A significant part of this cluster focuses on container shipping operations. Nguyen (2020) presents a quantitative model addressing uncertainty in container transport operations, categorizing risks into information, physical and payment-related groups, and analyzing them using a Fuzzy Rule-Based Bayesian Network (FRBN). Nguyen et al. (2021b) identify and model operational risks arising from blockchain adoption in container shipping, revealing 28 risks and 47 interdependencies through a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). Nguyen et al. (2022a) conduct a comprehensive review of operational risk assessment in container transport, highlighting conceptual differences in the definitions and classifications of ‘risk’ and emphasizing the increasing importance of collaborative risk reduction in the digital era. Nguyen et al. (2023) propose a methodological framework for the quantitative analysis of operational risks, focusing on uncertainty management through information generation, data collection, multi-source data integration and risk–uncertainty quantification. Nguyen (2021a) further examines the role of uncertainty by combining Bayesian probability theory with Evidential Reasoning (ER); findings show that high risks are mostly associated with physical flows, whereas information and financial risks exhibit higher uncertainty levels. Additional studies in this cluster investigate port supply chain risks in Nigeria (Nsikan et al. 2023), AIS-based models—using the Automatic Identification System (AIS)—for deep-learning-based collision-risk prediction in the Istanbul Strait (Oruç and Altan 2023), the adaptation of the Formal Safety Assessment (FSA) framework for container terminals (Pallis 2017), hybrid models combining grounded theory, Fault Tree Analysis (FTA) and Bayesian networks for shipfire risk (Wang et al. 2021), and a multi-stage failure model examining network resilience in liner shipping (Xu et al. 2024). Recent bibliometric reviews also identify research gaps in maritime cybersecurity and collision-risk studies (Yu et al. 2022; Yu et al. 2023).

The cluster brings together research that analyses operational hazards specific to shipbased activities—such as berthing, mooring, cargo handling and critical onboard procedures—and the methods used to model and manage these risks. These studies emphasize operational processes characterized by high uncertainty and aim to enhance the safety of vessel operations by developing analytical and decision-support frameworks. Common methodological approaches include fuzzy logic, Fault Tree Analysis (FTA), Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA), Fuzzy Fault Tree Analysis (FFTA) and hybrid risk-assessment models. Several studies integrate advanced modelling tools to address ship-specific safety challenges. Alkaç et al. (2025) analyze liquefaction risks in nickel ore transport using an integrated Fuzzy FTA and FMEA, showing that human errors account for 54% of total risk. Deng et al. (2025) propose a resilience-oriented framework to evaluate the performance of safety barriers in maritime operations. Erbas et al. (2024) conduct a systematic review of ship cybersecurity, comparing threat modelling and risk assessment methods and highlighting the lack of standardized frameworks, particularly for autonomous vessels. Goksu and Arslan (2023) present a Fuzzy FMEA-based quantitative safety analysis for berthing and unberthing operations, proposing preventive measures to reduce error consequences. Göksu et al. (2024) combine FTA and Bayesian Networks (BN) to assess the causes and interactions of power failures on ships. Other contributions adopt dynamic or hybrid analytical approaches. Hu et al. (2025) integrate Hidden Markov Models (HMM) and Dynamic Bayesian Networks (DBN) to evaluate the operational risks and traffic-system resilience of LNG-powered vessels. Kang et al. (2025) develop a risk assessment framework to predict leakage incidents in offshore LNG transfer systems. Kuzu (2023) combines fuzzy logic and DEMATEL to analyze factors leading to anchor losses and the causal relationships among them. Lin et al. (2023) merge FMEA with quantitative risk analysis for container port operations, applying the approach to four functional areas of Keelung Port in Taiwan. Osorio-Gomez and Manotas-Duque (2018) evaluate operational risks in third-party logistics (3PL) services in container shipping using Fuzzy QFD and TOPSIS. Sezer et al. (2023) examine manifold-operation risks on tanker vessels carrying hazardous liquid cargoes. Temel et al. (2024) assess self-heating risks in coal transport by integrating expert judgment with Fuzzy Bow-Tie Analysis. Uflaz et al. (2024) provide a quantitative assessment of maritime cybersecurity risks using a hybrid model combining FMECA, Dempster–Shafer theory and rule-based Bayesian networks. Xiao and Bai (2022) investigate how severe bottlenecks at Chinese ports propagate risks to global container trade using a D-Vine Copula Quantile Regression approach. Zhou et al. (2022) identify 28 key risks in container shipping using the PESTLE framework and evaluate them with a hybrid model integrating FMEA, Evidential Reasoning (ER) and rule-based Bayesian networks, concluding that economic, political and technological factors are the most critical threats.

This cluster brings together research addressing strategic decision-making, business continuity and financial uncertainties in the maritime sector. The studies primarily focus on freight rate volatility, fuel price fluctuations and the financial consequences of operational decisions. Overall, the cluster reflects efforts to enhance the financial resilience of maritime companies, support decision-making under uncertainty and help firms adapt to unpredictable market conditions. Several studies propose strategic frameworks to support organizational resilience. Akpinar and Özer-Çaylan (2023) develop a framework grounded in Complex Adaptive Systems (CAS), using Interpretive Structural Modeling (ISM) and MICMAC analysis to examine the interrelationships between CAS characteristics in maritime organizations. Alexandridis et al. (2018) propose a portfolio-based methodological framework for managing freight rate risk, drawing on the literature on freight derivatives. Berle et al. (2011) conceptualize the maritime transport system as a ‘transition mechanism,’ identifying critical functions and failure modes to support business continuity planning against low-probability, high-impact disruptions. Knapp and Heij (2017) analyze safety records and insurable values from approximately 130,000 ships to estimate Monetary Value at Risk (MVR), finding that tankers exhibit the highest risk exposure and container ships show the highest accident frequencies, alongside evidence of global underinsurance. Lai et al. (2020) apply the Define–Measure–Analyze–Improve–Control (DMAIC) methodology to propose a framework for managing various risk types in port logistics. Vander Hoorn and Knapp (2015) develop a multilayered assessment framework incorporating fleet heterogeneity, environmental conditions and uncertainty, demonstrating its application through a regional case study in Australia. Wang and Teo (2013) integrate fuel-price hedging and liner network replanning into a unified model to help container carriers manage fuel cost risks. Wu et al. (2018) investigate the vulnerability of the Maritime Silk Road container network to geopolitical disruptions and deliberate attacks, identifying critical chokepoints and proposing policies to enhance network resilience. Yang (2011) examines risk factors associated with the Container Security Initiative (CSI) in Taiwan’s maritime supply chain and proposes strategies such as loss prevention, loss mitigation and risk avoidance. Berle et al. (2011) treated maritime transport systems as a transition mechanism, defined failure modes arising from the loss of critical functions, and recommended developing business continuity planning against low-probability but high-impact disruptions.

This cluster addresses emerging risk types in maritime operations, particularly those driven by technological transformation, digitalization, blockchain applications and region- or route-specific geographic conditions. The studies highlight operational vulnerabilities associated with new technologies, quantify uncertainties through advanced modelling and integrate expert knowledge into decision-support systems. Several contributions also include region-specific case studies—such as Arctic routes or Southeast Asian operations—illustrating how local characteristics shape risk profiles. Akyuz and Celik (2014) propose a hybrid decision-making approach combining the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) and TOPSIS to assess the effectiveness of ship safety management systems. Baksh et al. (2018) develop a Bayesian Network (BN)-based model to estimate collision, capsizing and grounding probabilities for oil tankers navigating the Northern Sea Route. Fu et al. (2021) conduct a bibliometric and systematic review of Arctic shipping risk management, identifying environmental and vessel-related risk factors and modelling their interactions. Gu et al. (2023) present an integrated approach combining the Best Worst Method (BWM) and Fuzzy TODIM to enhance maritime supply chain resilience under scenarios such as port congestion, labor shortages and freight rate fluctuations. Several studies introduce innovative analytical and technological solutions. Guo et al. (2025) propose an anomaly-detection approach for vessel navigation data. Khan et al. (2025) analyze system and component failures in ammonia bunkering operations using Fuzzy Bayesian Networks (FBN). Li et al. (2023a) identify operational risks of Maritime Autonomous Surface Ships (MASS) and examine causal relationships among these risks using network analysis. Martinie et al. (2021) explore how human tasks influence the identification of cybersecurity threats in maritime supply chains. Merrick et al. (2022) develop a maritime accident early-warning system to support vessel-traffic operators. Nguyen et al. (2022b) identify potential operational risks associated with blockchain-integrated systems (BIS) in container shipping and quantitatively assess multi-event scenarios through expert interviews with terminal operators, carriers and freight forwarders. Nourmohammadi et al. (2023) apply big-data analytics and deep learning to predict short- and long-term accident risks for small and medium-sized vessels in South Korean waters. Xin et al. (2023) propose a clustering-based maritime traffic analysis method to detect high-risk multi-ship encounters, demonstrating its effectiveness using traffic data from the Ningbo–Zhoushan Port. Zhang et al. (2024) develop a hybrid STPA–Grey DEMATEL–TAISM (SgDT) framework to identify and model risk factors in automated container terminal operations, revealing 22 key risks and their causal relationships.

This cluster brings together data-driven research that aims to detect, classify and analyze maritime accidents and operational threats using dynamic, quantitative and machine-learning-based methods. Common themes include vessel traffic pattern analysis, anomaly detection, threat classification, human–machine interaction risks, accident prediction and early-warning system development. The studies collectively demonstrate how proactive, automated and data-centric approaches can enhance operational safety in maritime transport. Cao et al. (2024) analyze risk factors associated with four vessel types, bulk carriers, container ships, fishing vessels and oil tankers, using 910 accident reports, constructing ship-type-specific risk networks and proposing preventive strategies. Kuzu et al. (2019) assess accidents during mooring operations using Fuzzy Fault Tree Analysis (FFTA). Fan et al. (2025) develop a machine learning–enhanced Bayesian Network (BN) framework capable of handling incomplete and noisy datasets to predict the severity of maritime accidents. Fu et al. (2023) propose a system-theoretic framework integrating text mining, Bayesian Networks, fuzzy logic and expert judgement to identify accident scenarios, conduct risk assessment and recommend control strategies. Gulen et al. (2025) prioritized digital transformation strategies for proactive maritime safety management using Fuzzy AHP and TOPSIS. Jovanović et al. (2025) analyze the role of human factors in serious cargo-ship accidents (2010–2020) using Fault Tree Analysis (FTA) and Bayesian Networks, showing that both shipboard operations and shore-based management substantially influence accident likelihood. Liu et al. (2024a) integrate Interpretive Structural Modeling (ISM) with data-driven BN models to analyze safety risks in China’s Pearl River inland waterways. Li et al. (2024b) use dynamic Bayesian Networks to examine temporal changes in maritime accident patterns between 2012 and 2021, identifying risk intensification for large vessels, port areas, anchorage and maneuvering operations. Li et al. (2025) analyze 1,573 collision cases (2010–2023) using AI-supported clustering and pattern-recognition techniques to visualize collision mechanisms and risk similarities. Ma et al. (2025) examine risk evolution in typhoon-induced maritime accidents. Meng et al. (2024) integrate the N–K model with Bayesian Networks to quantify interactions among human, vessel, environmental and managerial factors in ship collisions in China, proposing risk mitigation strategies. Nguyen et al. (2018) propose a comprehensive quantitative model for container shipping operational risks (CSOR), integrating a Delphi-based communication platform, fuzzy logic and Bayesian Networks to assess uncertainty. Digitalization and sustainability related risks also appear in this cluster. Progoulakis et al. (2024) address cyber-physical threats emerging from increased integration of information and operational technologies in the maritime sector. Zhou and Yuen (2022) develop a Bayesian Network model to evaluate sustainability risks faced by container shipping companies, identifying 45 risks—including poor governance, insufficient crew training and weak environmental practices—and associated mitigation strategies.

This cluster brings together research focusing on operational risks that threaten the continuity of maritime logistics and supply chain systems, particularly in developing port environments. Key themes include port congestion, information flow disruptions, coordination gaps among stakeholders, and the management practices required to maintain supply chain resilience. The studies also highlight organizational mechanisms for enhancing resilience—such as risk feedback loops, periodic assessments, and investments in digitalization. Overall, the cluster synthesizes practical, field-based insights into maritime supply chain risk management and provides guidance particularly for developing port systems. Baştuğ et al. (2023) examined marketing-related risks in container transport arising from unexpected disruptions, using COVID-19 as an illustrative case, and proposed mitigation strategies based on literature review and Spherical Fuzzy Theory. Celik et al. (2010) developed a fuzzy extended fault tree (FFTA) model to analyze technical and organizational failures in maritime accident investigations. Chang et al. (2019) identified 18 risk mitigation strategies for container transport and evaluated their importance using fuzzy AHP based on financial, safety and reputational consequences. Chang et al. (2015) analyzed logistical risks in container transport, identifying 35 risk factors across information, physical and payment flows and ranking them via risk mapping. Jiang et al. (2017) investigated 16 risk factors in the maritime supply chain and used Interpretive Structural Modeling (ISM) to uncover their structural relationships and propose control strategies. Li et al. (2014) developed a numerical Ship Safety Index using static and dynamic data covering over 90% of the world fleet, generating relative risk scores for each vessel through binary logistic regression. Moslemi et al. (2016) analyzed risks in container logistics services in emerging Mediterranean markets through interviews and surveys, highlighting major risk drivers and their impacts. Müller and Haasis (2018) introduced a game-based learning approach to teach maritime logistics security risks and corresponding mitigation measures. Tatar et al. (2025) assessed ergonomic risks in port operations using the Fine-Kinney method integrated with spherical-fuzzy FUCOM and ARTASI techniques and proposed control actions. Vilko et al. (2019) explored risk visibility and control in multimodal maritime supply chains, revealing significant differences in actors’ risk awareness and management capabilities. Vilko and Hallikas (2012) analyzed risks in multimodal maritime supply chains between the Gulf of Finland and mainland Finland, proposing a new causal classification framework and evaluating delay impacts through Monte Carlo simulation. Finally, Yin et al. (2022) evaluated the risk management performance of maritime start-ups in China using fuzzy AHP and importance–performance analysis, highlighting financial and market-related improvement areas.

This cluster groups research focusing on operational safety threats and accident risk factors in maritime environments, particularly during vessel-specific and port-related operations such as berthing, mooring, maneuvering, or handling. The studies typically apply structured risk analysis techniques—including Bayesian Networks, fuzzy logic, FMEA and related models—to identify, model and mitigate accident-inducing factors. Several contributions also emphasize human error, information-system interactions, and other internal vulnerabilities. Overall, the cluster brings together applied and model-based frameworks designed to enhance operational safety and reduce accident likelihood. Abdulahi and Fan (2021) developed an operational risk scale for container transportation by examining risks across information, physical and payment flows, using exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis in the Ethiopian context. Arsham et al. (2013) analyzed grounding accidents in the Gulf of Finland and built evidencebased Bayesian Network models, demonstrating differences in structure-learning algorithms and cautioning against relying on a single algorithm. Liu et al. (2024b) assessed multi-ship collision risks in China using AIS-based modeling. Mazaheri et al. (2014) conducted a systematic review of grounding-risk models and proposed an information-driven modeling framework aligned with IMO’s Formal Safety Assessment (FSA). Montewka et al. (2014a) developed a proactive Bayesian Network risk model for RoPax collisions, validated through a Gulf of Finland case study. In a related work, Montewka et al. (2014b) argued that the FSA definition of risk is too narrow and proposed a broader perspective incorporating scenarios, probabilities, consequences and uncertainties. Nguyen and Wang (2018) identified container shipping operational risks from a logistics perspective and integrated FMEA with Fuzzy Rule-Based Bayesian Networks (FRBN) to support risk prioritization in a Vietnambased case study. Radwanski and Rutkowski (2022) examined risks in personnel transfers between offshore units, emphasizing equipment misuse and the need for preventive procedures. Van Dorp and Merrick (2011) combined simulation, accident data and expert judgment to analyze oil-spill risks, comparing different mitigation strategies such as escorts and traffic separation. Wu et al. (2019a) modeled collision consequences on the lower Yangtze River using Bayesian Networks. Ye et al. (2024) analyzed region-specific waterway risks on the Yangtze River using a twostage fuzzy rule-base and Bayesian Network model, offering insights for regional risk-management practices.

These works adopt a multidimensional perspective on operational risks in maritime transportation, emphasizing the interplay between environmental conditions, technological systems, and human factors. The studies typically integrate expert judgement, quantitative assessments, and uncertainty-based models—such as Bayesian Networks, Evidential Reasoning, risk mapping, and combined risk–uncertainty indices—to evaluate complex risk structures, particularly in container shipping. Topics addressed include cybersecurity vulnerabilities, inadequate infrastructure, inconsistencies in expert evaluations, inaccurate cargo declarations, fuel-cost volatility, and the operational challenges introduced by blockchain integration. Overall, the cluster reflects a holistic systems view, highlighting the interdependencies across environmental, technical, and human domains and contributing to safer, more resilient maritime operations. Acharya et al. (2017) analyzed the spatial distribution of maritime accidents in Korea using Geographic Information Systems (GIS), identifying accident hotspots through buffer and clustering analyses. Chang et al. (2023) proposed a two-stage framework combining Fault Tree Analysis (FTA) and Bayesian Networks for LNG transportation risk assessment on the China–Australia route, identifying natural forces, pandemics, piracy, terrorism, and LNG explosion risks as major threats. Demirel et al. (2024) developed a risk assessment framework for mooring operations at hydrocarbon berths using Bayesian Networks, fuzzy rule-based systems, and the Fuzzy Best Worst Method (FBWM). Erdem et al. (2023) examined the impact of human error on operational risks by integrating FTA with the SLIM under Interval Type-2 Fuzzy Logic. Liu and Frangopol (2018) conducted a probabilistic grounding-risk analysis considering economic, social, and environmental consequences, incorporating sustainability dimensions into risk evaluation. Macrae (2009) analyzed human and organizational error patterns in grounding and collision accidents based on 30 detailed investigation reports. Roh et al. (2018) assessed maritime supply chain security in Malaysian ports and waterways using a risk matrix, revealing vulnerabilities related to terrorism and piracy. Sun et al. (2023) proposed a software framework for risk management in smart ships. Tseng et al. (2018) used the AHP to identify major cargo-damage risk factors in container export operations in Taiwan, highlighting misdeclared cargo, improper packaging, and unreliable container–deck connections. Wu et al. (2019b) analyzed risks in China’s imported bauxite transportation using Markov Chains and cloud models to simulate risk evolution across voyage stages. Ünal and Arıcan (2025) examined critical risks in LNG/LPG tanker operations, including fire, explosion, and gas leakage, using Fuzzy Delphi, Fuzzy DEMATEL, and Fault Tree Analysis to prioritize mitigation strategies.
